title: Multilingual Dictation Without Unwanted Translation | OpenWispr
description: Wispr Flow users report the app spontaneously translating speech instead of transcribing it, and its auto-detect feature was removed. On-device transcription has a structurally different failure surface for this specific bug.
ogTitle: Multilingual dictation, without the surprise translation
ogDescription: A documented Wispr Flow bug: speaking Portuguese or Swedish and getting English text back, unrequested. Here's the structural reason on-device transcription doesn't share that specific failure path.
h1: Multilingual dictation, without the surprise translation
subhead: A specific, documented complaint about the category leader: speak in one language, and the app spontaneously translates to another without being asked. It's a real bug, named by real users, and worth understanding structurally before picking a dictation app for a multilingual workflow.

sections.heading: "As far as I know, live translation is not even a feature"
paragraphs: Two separate, dated organic complaints describe the same failure mode in Wispr Flow: "I speak English (mostly) and Portuguese… Wispr started to translate from one language to the other… After the ~20th time, I gave up and disabled Portuguese" (2026-06-15), and "Wispr Flow live translates when I speak Swedish into English. As far as I know, live translation is not even a feature" (2026-06-30). Wispr Flow's auto-detect was also removed at some point, which reportedly angered European users who relied on it to switch languages mid-session without manual configuration.

This isn't a claim that every cloud dictation product has this exact bug — it's a specific, sourced complaint about one product. It's included here because it points at a structural question worth asking about any dictation app you're evaluating for multilingual use: what happens between what you said and what lands on the page, and how many opportunities are there for that pipeline to do something you didn't ask for?

sections.heading: Fewer moving parts between your voice and the transcript
paragraphs: OpenWispr's on-device pipeline runs a speech model — NVIDIA Parakeet-TDT by default, or Whisper via whisper.cpp — directly on your device, with no network round-trip that could route audio through a different model, service version, or configuration than the one you started with. That's a structural property of the architecture, not a benchmarked claim about translation accuracy specifically — this page isn't asserting OpenWispr has been tested head-to-head against the exact failure mode described above, only that there's no cloud-side model swap or hidden mode change in the pipeline to produce it.

For context on language breadth elsewhere in this category: Muesli publishes a model table showing Parakeet v3 covering 25 languages and Nemotron 3.5 covering 100+ locales, on-device — a useful reference point for how far local models have come on multilingual coverage generally, separate from the specific translation bug discussed above.

faqs.q: Does Wispr Flow really mistranslate instead of transcribing?
faqs.a: Two separate, dated organic user reports describe exactly that — speaking Portuguese or Swedish and getting unrequested English translation back. Their auto-detect feature was also reportedly removed. This is a sourced complaint about that specific product, not a claim about the category as a whole.

faqs.q: Has OpenWispr been tested against this specific translation bug?
faqs.a: Not benchmarked head-to-head — this page makes a structural argument, not a tested-and-confirmed one. OpenWispr's on-device pipeline has no network round-trip that could swap models or modes mid-session, which is the mechanism most likely to produce that kind of surprise behavior, but that's an architectural observation, not a claim of measured multilingual accuracy.

faqs.q: How many languages does OpenWispr support?
faqs.a: It uses NVIDIA Parakeet-TDT by default or Whisper via whisper.cpp, both of which are multilingual models — but this page isn't citing a specific tested language count for OpenWispr itself. If exact language coverage matters for your use case, verify directly against the current model documentation on GitHub.

faqs.q: Which competitor publishes the clearest multilingual model information?
faqs.a: Muesli, among the apps covered in this research — a published table showing Parakeet v3 at 25 languages and Nemotron 3.5 at 100+ locales, on-device. See the OpenWispr vs Muesli comparison for the full picture, including where Muesli is ahead.

faqs.q: Is auto-detecting between multiple spoken languages mid-session supported?
faqs.a: This is a real, named gap for Wispr Flow specifically (auto-detect was removed). This page doesn't make a specific claim about OpenWispr's current auto-detect behavior — check current documentation on GitHub for the latest state.
